info.bio:
The Heartbreakers, también conocidos como Johnny Thunders and the Heartbreakers, fue una banda de punk y rock & roll formada en 1975 en Nueva York. La banda fue parte de la primera ola del punk rock.

Historia
La banda se formó cuando Johnny Thunders y Jerry Nolan abandonaron su antigua banda, New York Dolls en 1975, el mismo año en el que Richard Hell fue expulsado de la banda Television. Tras unos pocos conciertos se les unió el guitarrista Walter Lure, que había tocado en una banda llamada The Demons.

scenes.name: Punk neoyorquino del CBGB
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Ramones, Television, Patti Smith, Blondie, The Heartbreakers: una escena que, como advirtió James Wolcott en 1975 («Un impulso conservador en el nuevo underground del rock»), se presentaba como el retorno de algo perdido. Los Ramones agotan su idea en dos discos, los Heartbreakers son Dr. Feelgood con heroína y hasta Television bebe del acid rock de la costa oeste. La revista Punk de Legs McNeil proclama «¡Muerte a esa mierda disco!» y rechaza al hipster como «negro blanco».

scenes.name: Decadencia y glam-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El rock siempre tuvo un elemento de decadencia, amoralidad y obscenidad; entre los Cockettes (1968) y el Rocky Horror Picture Show (1974) se convierte en producto de masas. Gran Bretaña lo llama glam-rock: T.Rex lo inaugura y lo casa con el hard rock; David Bowie lo lleva a su cima comercial convirtiendo el marketing en arte (Ziggy Stardust, la trilogía berlinesa con Eno). En EE UU, Alice Cooper, Sparks, Iggy Pop y Lou Reed (Berlin, Metal Machine Music, New York). El glam y la decadencia preparan el punk: Mott The Hoople, Be Bop Deluxe, New York Dolls, Heartbreakers, Dictators, Modern Lovers de Jonathan Richman, Runaways.

podcast.title: Band Creation by Johnny Thunders
podcast.body: Johnny Thunders formed The Heartbreakers after his time as a member of the New York Dolls. "He began as a member of the New York Dolls before creating a bank called The Heartbreakers."

podcast.title: Early Performances at CBGB
podcast.body: The Heartbreakers were among the bands performing at CBGB by the summer of 1974. Their association with the club helped solidify its reputation as the epicenter for the emerging punk rock scene in New York City. "By the summer of 1974, Hilly's bar, now known just as CBGB to everyone, was hosting not just television, but the Ramones, Patty Smith, Suicide, Blondie, Talking Heads, the Heartbreakers, and a bunch of other groups."

podcast.title: Johnny Thunders' Character
podcast.body: Johnny Thunders, previously known as Johnny Volum and a former member of the New York Dolls, was an incurable alcoholic and junky. Despite his personal struggles, his distinctive attitude with a guitar and his compelling stage presence became a foundational blueprint for many future punk rockers. "Thunders was an incurable alcoholic and junky."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nancy Spungen as Groupie – Followed the Drummer to England
podcast.body: Nancy Spungen was a groupie of the Heartbreakers. She followed their drummer, Jerry Nolan, to England in an attempt to win him over, which eventually led to her encountering Sid Vicious. "When she followed Heartbreakers drummer Jerry Nolan to England to try and win him over, she stumbled onto this guy named Sid."

podcast.title: Television Spin-off and CBGB Scene Involvement
podcast.body: The Heartbreakers were identified as a "television spin-off band" and were part of the burgeoning CBGB scene, alongside Blondie, Suicide, and The Talking Heads, as the club became a central hub for new music. "CBGB was becoming the center of a new scene featuring bands with names like Blondie and Suicide and The Talking Heds and a television spin-off band called The Heartbreakers."

xref.title: Punk Fashion Inspiration (1975)
xref.body: During a 1975 trip to New York for a fashion fair, Malcolm McLaren took a detour to CBGBs, where he encountered Richard Hell, then bassist for The Heartbreakers. Hell, due to his poverty, wore ripped clothes held together with safety pins, a look McLaren misinterpreted as a "grand fashion statement," inspiring him to integrate safety pins into his own clothing designs back in England. "What drew Malcolm to Richard was a sense of style or what Malcolm thought to be Richard's sense of style because, well, you see, Richard was actually so poor that he'd wears clothing until they literally fell apart."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unwitting Punk Fashion Catalyst (1975)
xref.body: In 1975, while serving as the bassist for The Heartbreakers, Richard Hell met Malcolm McLaren at CBGBs in New York. Due to his impoverished circumstances, Hell wore his clothing until it literally fell apart, then used safety pins to hold the ripped scraps together. McLaren, misinterpreting this as a deliberate "grand fashion statement," adopted the idea and brought it back to England, where it became a cornerstone of nascent punk fashion. "What drew Malcolm to Richard was a sense of style or what Malcolm thought to be Richard's sense of style because, well, you see, Richard was actually so poor that he'd wears clothing until they literally fell apart. And once they did that, he'd hold the rip scraps of cloth together with safety pins."

xref.title: Early Life and Artistic Path
xref.body: Richard Hell, born Richard Myers in Kentucky, initially moved to New York with the ambition of becoming a poet before becoming captivated by the burgeoning punk scene at CBGB. "Richard, his real name was Richard Myers, was a member of several New York punk bands who hung out at CBGB, the brilliant television and the heartbreakers featuring the doomed Johnny Thunders, ex of the New York dolls. Richard was born in Kentucky but moved to New York with plans of being a poet."

xref.title: Early Residency at CBGB
xref.body: Television began playing a regular Sunday Night Residency at Hilly Crystal's bar, which would soon become widely known as CBGB. Their performances, starting around the same time that displaced artists from the Mercer Art Center began migrating to CBGB, helped establish the club as a hub for new music in New York City. "By the summer of 1974, Hilly's bar, now known just as CBGB to everyone, was hosting not just television, but the Ramones, Patty Smith, Suicide, Blondie, Talking Heads, the Heartbreakers, and a bunch of other groups."

xref.body: Stan Lynch, the drummer for Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, was a fan and provided assistance in recording her 1994 album, *Stop Messin with My Mind*. "She had a fan in Stan Lynch, the drummer for Tom Petty in the Heartbreakers, and he helped her record an album in 1994 called Stop Messin with My Mind."

xref.title: Formation of The Voidoids
xref.body: Richard Hell grew dissatisfied with The Heartbreakers and decided to form his own band, The Voidoids, a nihilistic punk group. The band's name was taken from a novel Richard was writing at the time. "But back to Richard. He grew tired of the heartbreakers very quickly and decided he needed to front his own band. They became known as the Voidoy's, a nihilistic punk group. The name came from the title of a novel Richard was working on at the time."

xref.title: Found Dead in New Orleans
xref.body: Johnny Thunders, the guitarist for the influential Protopunk band The New York Dolls and later his punk band The Heartbreakers, was found dead on April 23, 1991, at the St. Peter Guesthouse in New Orleans. He was known to have advanced leukemia and was a serious drug user. "On April 23, 1991, he was found dead at the St. Peter guesthouse in New Orleans."

xref.title: Musical Style
xref.body: Elvis Costello specialized in short, sharp, choppy songs, featuring a significant amount of rhythm guitar and a vaguely anti-corporate stance. This musical approach was similar to that of Talking Heads, Blondie, and Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, all of whom were categorized under the New Wave banner. "like the talking heads and blondie and Elvis Costello, Tom Petty specialized in short, sharp choppy songs with lots of rhythm guitar and vaguely anti-corporate stents."
